Steve Cohen's Point72 Asset Management filed its third-quarter 13F with the SEC on November 16, reporting about $90.0 billion in holdings at September 30, including options, according to 13f.info. That snapshot predates the Nasdaq Composite's 5.5% drop on November 5, its biggest one-day fall in 19 months, which left the index more than 10% below its October 6 record and confirmed a correction, Reuters reported. Chipmakers led the losses on fears of tougher AI regulation after Democrats won control of the US Congress, so the filing shows how Cohen's fund was positioned before the drop.

Inside Cohen's Latest Filing

The filing shows big changes near the top of the portfolio. Point72 raised its holding in a software giant from 31,522 shares at June 30 to 2,055,578 at September 30, and it roughly tripled its stake in a US chipmaker over the same period, according to its 13F filings. A 13F lists long stock positions and options at quarter-end, so it does not show when Point72 traded, at what price, or any short positions. Point72 also said on May 18 that Cohen remains chairman, CEO and co-chief investment officer, overseeing its day-to-day operations and investment strategies.

Filings like this one show where professional money sat before the drop, and our ranking of the AI stocks that billionaire investors hold in their portfolios looks at another slice of that money.

Hedge Funds Take a Hit

Cohen's fund is not the only one under pressure. Reuters reported on November 6 that JPMorgan estimated global hedge funds lost 3% in October, when the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.6%, its biggest monthly decline in 18 months. Goldman Sachs estimates showed multi-strategy managers, the group Point72 belongs to, fell 1.4% on November 5, and the research firm PivotalPath warned that the 10 largest multi-strategy funds hold increasingly similar positions, so their selling could hit many of the same securities.

The selling returned on November 17, when the S&P 500 fell 1% for a fourth straight loss and the Dow dropped 1.6%, according to the Associated Press. The Federal Reserve's minutes from its October 27-28 meeting, released the next day, showed that almost all participants judged further rate increases would likely be appropriate. Nasdaq futures rose nearly 2% on November 19 after a record-size AI developer public offering priced above its marketed range, Reuters reported, though LSEG data cited by Reuters show traders see a near-certainty of a quarter-point hike in December. That is the backdrop for the stocks below, which sit among Point72's largest common stock positions and also meet our screening criteria. For readers following the chip names, our list of the best semiconductor stocks to hold for the next decade covers more of the group.

Jensen Huang's return as CEO doesn't make Nvidia (NVDA) stock a Buy, despite the market's positive reaction. Shares of the leading semiconductor manufacturer jumped roughly 31.5% on November 23 after Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Huang with immediate effect. Yet the stock remains down roughly 31% over the past month following a steep sell-off.

Although Nvidia enjoys a long runway for growth, I believe investors should closely watch the regulatory scrutiny still surrounding the company. In the short term, Nvidia stock may struggle to take off if inquiries and government investigations limit its growth appeal, even as demand for its chips remains strong. As a result, I am turning Neutral on Nvidia because I believe its valuation already reflects both its strong chip demand and the regulatory and macro risks ahead.

An SEC Probe Threatens Nvidia's Reporting Structure

I believe investors should brace themselves for increased regulatory scrutiny in the coming months, which is one of the main reasons behind my Neutral stance on the company. There are early warning signs. On November 17, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is conducting a probe into Nvidia to look into its accounting practices and public disclosures to determine whether the chip giant has misled investors. On November 20, The New York Times (NYT) provided more details on this alleged SEC probe.

Specifically, the inquiry is looking into whether Nvidia's 2025 change in how it reports regional results has misled investors. Last year, the company switched from reporting revenue based on customer billing addresses to customer corporate headquarters. This shift entirely removed Singapore as a standalone geographic market for the company.

Given Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang, who was the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based Megaspeed, the SEC probe is likely to scrutinize this personal relationship. If Nvidia is found to have misled investors, the SEC may penalize the company with fines and even force it to restate its financials. Both outcomes will negatively affect shareholder sentiment.

The Government Probe Is Nowhere Near Complete

In addition to the SEC probe, I believe investors should pay close attention to the ongoing government probe of Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Before CEO Huang's reinstatement, President Trump wrote in a social media post, "Attorney General Todd Blanche has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

Stanley Druckenmiller, Bill Ackman and 7 Other Famous Investors Own Amazon. Here's Who Bought and Sold Recently ©Syammasfitria Studio and Tiger Lily from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Nine famous investors held Amazon at Sept. 30, per their latest 13Fs, and Stanley Druckenmiller's family office added 43% to its stake in the quarter.

Dan Loeb's Third Point sold all of its Amazon shares and opened new positions in Microsoft, Meta and Nvidia.

The sellers' best case is the cash: Amazon's free cash flow was a $42.4 billion outflow over the 12 months to Sept. 30.

With earnings expected to nearly double from 2025 to 2028 and the stock near its lowest forward P/E in five years, the numbers side with the buyers and the holders.

If you own Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), you're in famous company. Nine investors whose names regularly make headlines held the stock at Sept. 30, according to their 13Fs for the third quarter, filed from Nov. 6 to Nov. 16.

Most of them barely touched their stakes. Two made real moves, in opposite directions.

Druckenmiller added, and Loeb sold out

Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne Family Office raised its stake 43% in the quarter, to 772,600 shares from 541,600. At Sept. 30, that was $192 million of stock, 4.6% of the $4.15 billion of US stocks in its 13F and its third-largest position. Duquesne also held call options on Amazon with a notional value of $114 million.

Dan Loeb's Third Point went the other way. It held 1.75 million Amazon shares worth $417 million at June 30, 9.0% of its 13F stocks then, and none by Sept. 30. The same 13F shows new positions in Meta, Nvidia and Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), so Loeb is still betting on AI's biggest names, just not on Amazon.

TIKR tracks 62 analysts on Amazon. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Amazon, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Amazon's Analyst Ratings

Most of the rest sat tight

Here's where all nine stood at Sept. 30:

Source: each fund's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026. Values at Sept. 30 prices.

Amazon is a top-two holding for four of the nine. It's Seth Klarman's biggest position at Baupost, and Peter Thiel's stake makes up 26.8% of a small 13F that holds $460 million of US stocks in five positions. Tepper and Soros each trimmed about a tenth of their shares, and Amazon is still No. 2 at both. Cathie Wood's ARK added 7% in the quarter, though it has trimmed its flagship fund's stake since. Since then, Amazon has slipped 2% from its Sept. 30 price.

The sellers' best case is the cash

If you're looking for a reason to sell, Amazon's cash flow is it. In the third quarter, AWS revenue rose 39% to $46.0 billion, and operating income rose to $28.1 billion from $17.4 billion a year earlier. But building all that AI capacity costs a fortune. Free cash flow was a $42.4 billion outflow over the 12 months to Sept. 30, against a $14.8 billion inflow a year earlier, and Amazon held its 2026 capital spending plan at about $220 billion. Analysts don't expect free cash flow to turn positive again until 2028.

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) shares rose 1.3% to $127.44 at the 4:00 p.m. ET close on November 25, after the Federal Communications Commission granted conditional approval for up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business. The network, called Starmind, will operate between 500 and 1,002 kilometers using laser links, and won approval over objections from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Sign with SPCX.

Is SPCX fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The license comes with a long runway. SpaceX must launch its first operational satellite by November 25, 2033, deploy 10% of the network by 2035, half by 2038 and the rest by 2040, Via Satellite reported from the order. Each satellite's compute payload averages 175 kilowatts, with a ceiling of 250 kilowatts. Debris plans for satellites above 600 kilometers still need approval. FCC Chair Brendan Carr called the decision a bold new frontier for computing infrastructure.

At full build-out, 1 million satellites at 175 kilowatts each would add up to 175 gigawatts of compute power, though that is a license ceiling, not a funded plan. SpaceX plans to start launches in 2027, so revenue is years away. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of just 21/100, flagging weak profitability and an earnings base that does not yet support a $1.73 trillion valuation. That gap is the core risk: the FCC handed SpaceX an option, not cash flow. The next test is the first Starmind launch and a debris plan that clears the FCC.

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) shares jumped 3.4% to $609.89 at the 4:00 p.m. ET close on November 25, after Fortune reported that Amazon is in talks that could let Meta's Muse AI agent back onto its marketplace. The reversal was sharp. Shares had dropped 3.74% to $567.75 earlier in the session, so the close marked a 7.4% swing off the low.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Sign with META.

META GF Value chart

Muse is a personal AI agent that books reservations and buys products for its users. Meta launched it in the U.S. in September, and more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set it up by October, according to TradingKey coverage of the talks. Amazon blocked the agent in September, citing its user agreements. Any deal would need sign-off from both chief executives, and both companies declined to comment. Andy Jassy has said Amazon is open to outside shopping agents if they deliver fair value in return.

A deal would give Muse access to the largest U.S. online store, the difference between an agent that recommends and one that completes purchases. That is the monetization path investors want after heavy AI spending, though terms could include fees or data-sharing that dilute the payoff. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 99/100, with elite profitability, a sturdy balance sheet and solid momentum. GF Value of $892.33 implies a 31.7% discount and a "significantly undervalued" label, suggesting the market still weighs Meta's capex more heavily than its earning power. The next test is a signed agreement; until then, Wednesday's rally rests on a report, not a contract.

Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN) shares fell 3.12% to $244.43 at the 4:00 p.m. ET close on November 25, after Bernstein warned that web activity on usage-based cloud platforms, including AWS, ran about 16% below third-quarter levels in mid-to-late November. Warning! GuruFocus has detected 4 Warning Signs with AMZN.

AMZN GF Value chart

Bernstein said the slowdown could trim AWS revenue growth by several hundred basis points in the first quarter of 2027. The timing is awkward. AWS sales rose 39% to $46.0 billion in the third quarter, and operating income climbed 55% to $17.8 billion, about 63% of Amazon's $28.1 billion total. Andy Jassy has pointed to AWS growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Meanwhile, Amazon guides to roughly $220 billion of 2026 cash capex, and trailing 12-month free cash flow was an outflow of $42.4 billion.

With AWS producing nearly two-thirds of operating profit, a few hundred basis points of slower growth would land squarely on earnings, while capex stays locked in. That is the tension: Amazon is spending as if 40% growth is assured, and Bernstein's data suggests usage is cooling. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 94/100, combining strong profitability with a solid but not spotless balance sheet. At a GF Value of $260.46, shares trade at a 6.2% discount and screen as fairly valued, which leaves little cushion if growth disappoints. The next checkpoint is whether December usage data confirms the dip; the real verdict comes with fourth-quarter results, when AWS growth either holds near 40% or starts to bend.

title: Goldman Sachs sends strong signal on Amazon stock before Black Friday
detail:
Goldman Sachs sends strong signal on Amazon stock before Black Friday
Moz Farooque
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 1:17 PM EST 5 min read
GS
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Every Black Friday, my online shopping routine follows the same script. 

I tell myself I'm grabbing just a few gifts, but by the time the cardboard boxes stack up by the front door, half my cart is filled with everyday basics, including coffee pods, paper towels, and laundry detergent, tossed in because one-click next-day shipping makes it all effortless.

If your own Amazon (AMZN) cart resembles mine, you are witnessing firsthand what has Goldman Sachs analysts leaning in hard. 

Just days ahead of official Black Friday shopping and Amazon's flagship cloud conference, in a note shared with me, Goldman Sachs just delivered a high-conviction signal on Amazon stock. As nervous traders continue to punish Big Tech over hefty spending bills, Goldman argues the market is misreading two powerful profit engines hiding in plain sight.

Inside Goldman Sachs' $370 retail thesis for Amazon stock

Goldman Sachs analyst Eric Sheridan and his team reiterated a Buy rating on Amazon, keeping its stock on the firm's Americas Conviction List, and reiterating its $370 12-month price target. That call implies around a 46.7% upside from Amazon stock's November 24 finish at $252.29.

Sheridan didn't mince words about the setup, stating that Amazon's pricing setup "…leaves the stock as the most compelling risk/reward in our mega/large cap coverage from current levels."

Read more: Amazon, Walmart, and Target's holiday returns hide a catch

A core pillar of that call stems from changes in everyday shopping habits.

According to the bank, instead of losing shoppers to outside chatbots, Amazon's first-party AI assistant, Alexa for Shopping, generated around $12 billion in incremental sales across over 300 million users in 2025. It is projected to climb 33% year over year to $16 billion or more across 400 million users in 2026.

Shoppers using it convert at 16%, a 60% lift over the 10% e-commerce baseline, while new "Shop Direct" and "Buy for Me" features allow Amazon to complete purchases even on external brand sites.

Meanwhile, fresh grocery and Everyday Essentials grew at about three times the rate of other categories and now account for 50% of all U.S. units sold. 

That's backed up by a brand new Uber Eats Prime perk across 10,000 cities and a high-frequency "halo effect" in which active grocery shoppers spend over twice as much across non-grocery categories.

Lower-priced staples ended up compressing Q3 stores contribution profit by around 220 basis points, but Goldman argues investors are overlooking automation. Amazon is now running more than 1 million fulfillment robots, potentially cutting per-unit cost-to-serve by around 13% by 2030, from $6.38 to $5.50.
